notes.headline: Take-Two: bookings fall 18% in the quiet before GTA VI, as pre-orders reach “unprecedented levels” ten days from launch
notes.takeaway: Net bookings fell 18% to $1.60 billion and Take-Two lost $0.29 a share, a narrower loss than the $0.86 analysts expected. With Grand Theft Auto VI ten days from release and pre-orders at record levels, management reiterated full-year bookings guidance of $8.0 to $8.2 billion, and the shares rose 4.5%.
results: Take-Two Interactive reported net bookings — its main operating measure of sales — of $1.60 billion for the quarter ended September 30, down 18% from $1.96 billion a year earlier, which had included the launch of Borderlands 4. Recurrent consumer spending, from in-game purchases and add-ons, fell 9% and made up 81% of bookings. GAAP revenue was $1.50 billion against $1.77 billion.

The GAAP net loss narrowed to $54.0 million, or $0.29 a share, from $133.9 million, or $0.73, a year earlier, and was much smaller than the loss analysts had forecast. The largest contributors were NBA 2K, the Grand Theft Auto series, Zynga’s mobile games Toon Blast, Match Factory! and Empires & Puzzles, the Borderlands franchise and Red Dead Redemption.

On the company’s own management basis, which adds back the change in deferred revenue, stock compensation and acquisition amortisation, adjusted EBITDA was $92 million for the quarter, using an 18% tax rate and 188 million diluted shares for its per-share figures.
mgmt: Chairman and chief executive Strauss Zelnick said the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI was ten days away, with pre-orders continuing to reach unprecedented levels, and that the company expects to deliver a historic year. Take-Two reiterated its outlook for fiscal 2027 net bookings of $8.0 to $8.2 billion and gave its first guidance for the December quarter, which will contain the launch.

Zelnick said the company is confident it can build on the year by releasing new hits, exploring new business opportunities, expanding its geographic footprint and pursuing acquisitions, all aimed at greater earnings power.
view: This report was never going to be about the September quarter. Take-Two has spent years with depressed earnings while funding the most expensive entertainment product ever made, and every analyst model hinges on one date: November 19, 2026, the release of GTA VI. Grand Theft Auto V has sold more than 200 million copies and still earns money twelve years after release, largely through GTA Online. If GTA VI follows a similar path, it will transform Take-Two’s profitability for the rest of the decade.

The language matters here. Public companies rarely describe pre-orders as unprecedented unless they mean it, and reiterating $8.0–$8.2 billion of bookings ten days before launch, with pre-order data in hand, is a strong signal. The guidance implies the second half alone will bring in more than $5 billion of bookings, most of it from one title. The company also had the discipline not to raise guidance before a single copy shipped, leaving room to beat.

The risks are execution and expectations. The game has already been delayed twice, and any major technical problems at launch would hurt both sales and the long-term online business, which is where the real value lies. Expectations are also enormous: the shares trade on next year’s earnings rather than this year’s losses, at roughly 35 times analysts’ forecasts for the year to March 2028. The real test is not launch-week sales — those will almost certainly set records — but whether GTA Online’s successor can generate the recurring spending that sustained GTA V for over a decade.
notes.watch: Watch first-week and first-month sales figures for GTA VI, the December-quarter bookings against guidance, the timing of the new online mode, and the first outlook for fiscal 2028 in May.
